title: 'I Am Everywhere'
script: This is Door 81. 'I Am Everywhere'. It is verse 104 of the old text. In our plain words: let go of living only inside this body. With a firm mind, and looking at nothing else, contemplate: I am everywhere. Then, the old text says, happiness comes. Singh says there are two sides to it. First, I am not only this body, this place, this time. Then, I am everywhere. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If this feels disorienting, feel the body's weight on the floor, and open your eyes. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] First notice the habit of feeling: I am here, inside this body. Loosen it. Then, steadily, contemplate: I am everywhere. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Not only here. Let the edges of here loosen. [pause 16s] I am everywhere. Steady. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest, and notice any gladness that comes. [pause 16s] Release the attention. Feel the weight of the body on its support. Open the eyes when ready.

title: Knowing and Willing in Everything, and Attention to the Link
script: This is Door 82. Knowing and Willing in Everything, and Attention to the Link. It is verses 105 and 106 of the old text. In our plain words: the knowing and the willing in me are not in me alone. They arise in everything, even in a clay pot. Contemplating this, you become all-pervading. And the next verse adds: everyone knows things, but a yogi stays aware of the link between the knower and the known. Singh counts both verses as one door. Wallis counts them as two. The school follows Singh. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is a contemplation, not a belief to force on yourself. Keep it light. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] First, feel your own knowing and willing. Then bring to mind a simple thing, a pot or a stone, and sense the same knowing in it. Then notice the link between you, the knower, and it, the known. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Knowing here. The same in the pot, the stone. [pause 16s] Now the link. Knower, known, and the link between. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in that link. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: The Same Awareness in Another's Body
script: This is Door 83. The Same Awareness in Another's Body. It is verse 107 of the old text. In our plain words: feel awareness in another's body just as in your own. Let go of concern for your own body, and you become all-pervading. The verse says this happens within days. That is the old text's own claim. The school promises nothing. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is an inner contemplation. It is never a reason to cross anyone's boundaries, of body or of feeling. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] First feel the awareness alive in your own body. Then bring to mind someone nearby, or someone you know, and feel the same awareness alive in them, just as clearly. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Awareness alive here. [pause 16s] The same awareness, alive in them, just as clearly. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Let concern for this body rest a while. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: A Supportless Mind That Builds No Thoughts
script: This is Door 84. A Supportless Mind That Builds No Thoughts. It is verse 108 of the old text. In our plain words: make the mind rest on no support, and don't build up thoughts. Then the self becomes the supreme self, and that, the old text says, is Bhairava. Bhairava is the old text's name for Shiva as the wide, open awareness. Singh says the supports can be outer, like objects, or inner, like images and ideas. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If this starts to feel like effort, rest attention lightly on the breath for a while. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Let the mind lean on nothing. No object, no image, no idea. When a thought appears, don't build on it. Let it pass. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Leaning on nothing. [pause 16s] A thought comes. Don't build. Let it pass. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the open awareness that remains. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: I Share the Qualities of Śiva
script: This is Door 85. I Share the Qualities of Śiva. It is verse 109 of the old text. In our plain words: 'The supreme knows all, does all, and is everywhere. I am that, with the same qualities as Shiva.' Through the firmness of this knowing, the old text says, you become Shiva. Singh calls this the first step of recognition: seeing your own nature under the mask of a small self. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is recognising your own nature. It is not a claim to special powers. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Three qualities. Knowing. Doing. Being everywhere. Recognise them, in small measure, in yourself. You know. You act. Your awareness reaches out. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] You know. You act. Your awareness reaches. [pause 16s] The same qualities. Recognise them, firmly. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in that recognition. [pause 16s] Release the attention. Feel the weight of the body on its support. Open the eyes when ready.

title: Waves from Water: The World Arising from Me
script: This is Door 86. Waves from Water: The World Arising from Me. It is verse 110 of the old text. In our plain words: as waves rise from water, flames from fire, and rays from the sun, so all the many waves of the world rise from me, from Bhairava. Singh calls this the second step of recognition: the world, too, is your own expression. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is about awareness. It is not a claim to control events. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Picture waves rising from water. Many forms, one water. Then let sounds, sights and thoughts be waves rising from your own awareness. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Waves from water. Flames from fire. Rays from the sun. [pause 16s] Sounds, sights, thoughts. Waves from your own awareness. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest as the water. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: Whirling Until Falling (Classical)
script: This is Door 87. Whirling Until Falling (Classical). It is verse 111 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. The old text describes whirling the body round and round, then swiftly falling to the ground. When the agitation stops, it says, the supreme state appears. Singh reads it together with the next verse: both are about the stillness at the end of a great stirring. Some translators read wandering for a long time instead of whirling. The school never teaches spinning or falling. Don't whirl until you are dizzy or fall. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 60. Gentle rocking or swaying, where a slow, easy movement brings calm, and you rest in it. [pause 3s] Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.

title: When the Mind Gives Up: The Stillness After an Impasse
script: This is Door 88. When the Mind Gives Up: The Stillness After an Impasse. It is verse 112 of the old text. In our plain words: when the mind can't grasp what it reaches for, or simply doesn't know, it dissolves. At the end of the stirring that follows, the old text says, Bhairava's form appears. Singh pictures questioning or doubt wearing itself out. We rehearse here with a question that can't be answered in words. That is a school device; the verse itself is about such moments as they come. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is letting go of mental effort. It is not ignoring real problems. Come back to them later, rested. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Ask a question the mind can't answer. Where was this thought just before it came? Look, and let the mind fail to find it. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] The mind reaches. It can't grasp. Stop pushing. [pause 16s] Let the not-knowing be complete. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the stillness after. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: Unmoving Eyes; Ears and Lower Openings Closed (Classical)
script: This is Door 89. Unmoving Eyes; Ears and Lower Openings Closed (Classical). It is verses 113 and 114 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. These two verses describe the eyes kept completely still, and then closing the ears and the lower openings of the body while meditating on an inner, unstruck sound. Singh counts the two verses as one door. Wallis counts them as two. Singh links the still eyes to an unblinking, open-eyed gaze. The school doesn't teach any of this. No unblinking gaze, no pressing on the ears, and no contracting of the body. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 66. When a sense is blocked. There you rest your palms lightly over your ears, or simply let the eyes rest shut, and notice the quiet space that opens. [pause 3s] Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.

title: Gazing into a Deep Well (Classical)
script: This is Door 90. Gazing into a Deep Well (Classical). It is verse 115 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. The old text describes standing above a well or a great chasm and gazing down into it. For a mind free of busy thoughts, it says, the mind dissolves at once. Singh adds that the depth brings giddiness and fear, which jolt the mind out of its usual track. The school never teaches standing at an edge or a height. Don't practise at wells, cliffs or drops. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 36. Gazing into the space inside a pot. There you look safely into the hollow of a bowl, leave the walls aside, and rest in the space inside. [pause 3s] Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.

title: Wherever the Mind Goes
script: This is Door 91. Wherever the Mind Goes. It is verse 116 of the old text. In our plain words: wherever the mind goes, outward or inward, there is the state of Shiva. Since that state is everywhere, where could the mind go? Singh says there is no need to struggle to concentrate. Whatever draws the mind, take it as that very state. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If a difficult memory comes, you can open your eyes and rest on something neutral. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Let the mind go where it goes. A sound. A colour. A memory. Don't pull it back. Wherever it lands, rest there, as in the sacred. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Wherever it lands. Rest there. [pause 16s] It moves. Rest where it lands again. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Nowhere to go but here. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: Consciousness Shining Through the Senses
script: This is Door 92. Consciousness Shining Through the Senses. It is verse 117 of the old text. In our plain words: wherever consciousness shows itself through the senses, it is consciousness alone that carries what is perceived. So the mind dissolves into it, and you come to fullness. Singh's picture is a mirror. A reflection in it is nothing but the mirror. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If sensations are strong or unpleasant, begin with a neutral one, like a soft sound. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Keep your eyes open or closed, as you like. [pause 4s] Notice a sensation as it arrives. A sound. A colour. The touch of air. Feel it as awareness itself, taking that form, like a reflection that is only the mirror. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] A sound. Only awareness, in that form. [pause 16s] A touch. A colour. The same. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the fullness. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: Sneezes, Shocks and Sudden Moments
script: This is Door 93. Sneezes, Shocks and Sudden Moments. It is verse 118 of the old text. In our plain words: at the start and end of a sneeze, in fear, in sorrow, at a deep sigh, in flight, in curiosity, at the start and end of hunger: that state is full of the being of the absolute. Singh says any sudden jolt throws ordinary awareness back to its depth. Readings differ on one word: Singh hears a deep sigh, others a deep pit. This door is for such moments as they come in daily life. Sitting here, we rehearse only with small sudden moments, like an unexpected sound, or a flicker of curiosity. Never stir up fear, sorrow or hunger to practise. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Only notice these moments as they come by themselves. If fear or sorrow is overwhelming, reach out to people you trust. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Keep your eyes as they are. [pause 4s] Wait, relaxed, for a small sudden moment. A sound you didn't expect. A swallow. A flicker of curiosity. Notice the brief opening it makes. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] A small jolt. The brief opening. [pause 16s] Rest in that opening for a moment. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Let the next sudden moment remind you of this door. [pause 16s] Carry on with your day. Let the next sudden moment be a reminder of this door.

title: Seeing a Familiar Place, Letting Memories Go
script: This is Door 94. Seeing a Familiar Place, Letting Memories Go. It is verse 119 of the old text. In our plain words: when a place is seen and memories come, release the mind from them. Let the body be without support, and the Lord spreads forth. Singh says to let the remembered things go and rest in the plain experience of seeing. Wallis says it is a place you have been before. The room you are in now will do. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If a place carries painful memories, don't force this. Choose a neutral place, or come back to it with support. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Keep your eyes open, softly. [pause 4s] Look around this familiar room. Notice the memories it brings up. Let each one go, without following it. See the room as it is, right now. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] A memory comes. Let it go. Just the room, now. [pause 16s] Feel the body as if resting on nothing. Open. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in plain seeing. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: Placing the Gaze, Then Withdrawing It
script: This is Door 95. Placing the Gaze, Then Withdrawing It. It is verse 120 of the old text. In our plain words: rest the gaze on some object. Then slowly withdraw it, and with it the knowing of the object, and the mind too. Then, the old text says, you become a home of the void. Singh also mentions an unblinking gaze. That isn't in the verse, and the school doesn't teach it. Blink naturally. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Blink whenever you need to. Never strain the eyes. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Set one simple thing in front of you, like a cup or a stone. Keep your eyes open and soft, resting on that simple thing. [pause 4s] Rest the gaze on the simple thing. Later, slowly withdraw. First the eyes soften or close. Then the thought of the thing fades. Then the mind itself settles back. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] The gaze resting on the thing. [pause 16s] Now soften or close the eyes. Let the thought of it fade. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Let the mind settle back, into open emptiness. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: The Understanding Born of Devotion
script: This is Door 96. The Understanding Born of Devotion. It is verse 121 of the old text. In our plain words: the understanding that comes from overflowing devotion, in one free of grasping, is the power of Shiva. Contemplate it constantly, and you are Shiva. Singh says devotion is not only flowers and incense. It is seeing the sacred in all life. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Devotion here is inner and freely given. It never asks you to give up your judgement, your boundaries, or the people in your life. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or keep them soft. [pause 4s] Turn toward whatever is sacred to you. The divine. Life itself. A teacher, or an ideal. Let devotion well up, wanting nothing from it. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Devotion, wanting nothing. [pause 16s] Notice the quiet, clear understanding it brings. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in that understanding, and return to it often. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.
